claim: At 7 weeks of development, the glycoprotein 2 (GP2) marks a multipotent cell population that will differentiate into the acinar, ductal or endocrine lineages.
source: Here, we reconstructed human fetal pancreatic differentiation using cell surface markers. We demonstrate that at 7weeks of development, the glycoprotein 2 (GP2) marks a multipotent cell population that will differentiate into the acinar, ductal or endocrine lineages.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data showing GP2+ population at 7WD (Figure 2C), transcriptomic analysis showing GP2+ cells express markers of multiple lineages (Figure 3B), and temporal tracking of GP2+ population differentiation (Figure 2D,E)

claim: Development towards the acinar lineage is paralleled by an increase in GP2 expression.
source: Development towards the acinar lineage is paralleled by an increase in GP2 expression.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry showing emergence of GP2hi population (Figure 2C,D) and RT-qPCR showing acinar markers enriched in GP2hi population (Figure 4A)

claim: A subset of the GP2+ population undergoes endocrine differentiation by down-regulating GP2 and CD142 and turning on NEUROG3.
source: Conversely, a subset of the GP2+ population undergoes endocrine differentiation by down-regulating GP2 and CD142 and turning on NEUROG3, a marker of endocrine differentiation.
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR showing NEUROG3 expression in GP2- population (Figure 4C) and flow cytometry showing CD142 downregulation during endocrine differentiation (Figure 5C)

claim: Endocrine maturation progresses by up-regulating SUSD2 and lowering ECAD levels.
source: Endocrine maturation progresses by up-regulating SUSD2 and lowering ECAD levels.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry showing SUSD2 upregulation in Elow population (Figure 5B,C) and temporal analysis showing ECAD decrease during endocrine differentiation (Figure 2C)

claim: In vitro differentiation of pancreatic endocrine cells derived from human pluripotent stem cells mimics key in vivo events.
source: Finally, in vitro differentiation of pancreatic endocrine cells derived from human pluripotent stem cells mimics key in vivo events.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry and RT-qPCR comparing hPSC-derived cells to fetal pancreas showing similar marker expression patterns (Figure 7B-F)

claim: Beta cell replacement holds immense promises for diabetic patients and current strategies have reached major milestones.
source: Beta cell replacement holds immense promises for diabetic patients and current strategies have reached major milestones (Pagliuca et al., 2014; Russ et al., 2015; Rezania et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies on beta cell replacement strategies

claim: A more detailed understanding of beta cell development in human is required to generate unlimited functional human beta cells.
source: However, it is well accepted that a more detailed understanding of beta cell development in human is required to generate unlimited functional human beta cells (Johnson, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to published review on beta cell development

claim: The adult pancreas is composed of acinar cells that excrete enzymes into the duodenum through a ductal tree, and of endocrine cells (approximately 1% of the total pancreatic cells) that are clustered together forming the islets of Langerhans.
source: The adult pancreas is composed of acinar cells that excrete enzymes into the duodenum through a ductal tree, and of endocrine cells (approximately 1% of the total pancreatic cells) that are clustered together forming the islets of Langerhans.
evidence: Based on established anatomical and physiological knowledge of pancreatic structure

claim: The endocrine cells secrete hormones such as insulin (beta cells), glucagon (alpha cells) somatostatin (delta cells), pancreatic polypeptide (gamma cells) and ghrelin (epsilon cells).
source: The endocrine cells secrete hormones such as insulin (beta cells), glucagon (alpha cells) somatostatin (delta cells), pancreatic polypeptide (gamma cells) and ghrelin (epsilon cells).
evidence: Based on established knowledge of pancreatic endocrine cell types and their hormone products

claim: The pancreas develops from the primitive gut tube that evaginates into a dorsal and a ventral anlage.
source: The pancreas develops from the primitive gut tube that evaginates into a dorsal and a ventral anlage (Pan and Wright, 2011; Jennings et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published reviews on pancreatic development

claim: Multipotent epithelial pancreatic progenitors co-expressing the transcription factors PDX1 and NKX6-1 proliferate upon signals (such as FGF10) from the adjacent mesenchyme and subsequently differentiate into the acinar, ductal and endocrine lineages.
source: Multipotent epithelial pancreatic progenitors co-expressing the transcription factors PDX1 and NKX6-1 (Nelson et al., 2007; Cebola et al., 2015) proliferate upon signals (such as FGF10) from the adjacent mesenchyme (Bhushan et al., 2001) and subsequently differentiate into the acinar, ductal and endocrine lineages.
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies on pancreatic progenitor cells and their differentiation

claim: Endocrine commitment is initially marked by the expression of a basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor, NEUROG3, and followed by the expression of the mature endocrine markers.
source: Endocrine commitment is initially marked by the expression of a basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor, NEUROG3, and followed by the expression of the mature endocrine markers (Gradwohl et al., 2000; Gu et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies on NEUROG3 and endocrine differentiation

claim: Due to the difficulties associated with procuring staged human fetal tissues and the limited tools for their analysis, few data on human development is available and the majority of knowledge on tissue development derives from animal models.
source: Due to the difficulties associated with procuring staged human fetal tissues and the limited tools for their analysis, few data on human development is available and the majority of knowledge on tissue development derives from animal models.
evidence: Based on general knowledge of limitations in human developmental biology research

claim: Studies on human pancreatic development demonstrate similarities but also differences between rodent and human pancreatic development.
source: Theses studies demonstrate similarities but also differences between rodent and human pancreatic development (Scharfmann et al., 2013; Jennings et al., 2015; Nair and Hebrok, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published comparative studies on rodent and human pancreatic development

claim: EPCAM expression is restricted to the epithelium in the human fetal pancreas.
source: EPCAM expression is restricted to the epithelium in the human fetal pancreas
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry showing EPCAM+ cells express PDX1 (Figure 1B) and flow cytometry showing PDX1 and NKX6-1 expression restricted to EPCAM+ fraction (Figure 1C-F)

claim: EPCAM can be used to purify human fetal pancreatic epithelial fraction enriched in pancreatic progenitors.
source: We tested if EPCAM can be used to purify human fetal pancreatic epithelial fraction enriched in pancreatic progenitors.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry and RT-qPCR showing PDX1 and NKX6-1 expression restricted to CD45-CD31-EPCAM+ fraction (Figure 1C-F)

claim: EPCAM+ cells expressed PDX1 in human fetal pancreatic sections at 9WD.
source: Immunohistochemistry analysis of human fetal pancreatic sections showed that EPCAM+ cells expressed PDX1 (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry image showing co-localization of EPCAM and PDX1 (Figure 1B)

claim: PDX1 and NKX6-1 were co-expressed in the CD45-CD31-EPCAM+ fraction at 9.4WD.
source: FACS analysis demonstrated that PDX1 and NKX6-1 were co-expressed in the CD45-CD31-EPCAM+ fraction (Figure 1C–E).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry plots showing PDX1 and NKX6-1 co-expression in EPCAM+ cells (Figure 1C-E)

claim: PDX1 and NKX6-1 expressions were restricted to the CD45-CD31-EPCAM+ fraction.
source: RT-qPCR analysis on sorted fractions confirmed that PDX1 and NKX6-1 expressions were restricted to the CD45-CD31-EPCAM+ fraction (Figure 1F)
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data showing PDX1 and NKX6-1 expression only in EPCAM+ fraction (Figure 1F)

claim: The CD45-CD31-EPCAM- fraction did not express pancreatic markers and most likely represent the mesenchymal pancreatic fraction.
source: whereas the CD45-CD31-EPCAM- fraction did not express pancreatic markers and most likely represent the mesenchymal pancreatic fraction (later referred as population M) (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR showing no pancreatic marker expression in EPCAM- fraction (Figure 1F) and inference based on marker expression pattern

claim: A combination of the cell surface markers EPCAM, CD45, and CD31 can be used to purify the human fetal pancreatic epithelial fraction.
source: These results suggest that a combination of the cell surface markers EPCAM, CD45, and CD31 can be used to purify the human fetal pancreatic epithelial fraction.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry and RT-qPCR data showing pancreatic progenitor markers restricted to CD45-CD31-EPCAM+ fraction (Figure 1)

claim: GP2 was identified as a novel cell surface marker of the immature pancreatic progenitor cells derived from hPSC.
source: Recently, GP2 was identified as a novel cell surface marker of the immature pancreatic progenitor cells derived from hPSC (Ameri et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study on GP2 as a marker of pancreatic progenitors

claim: ECAD levels are tightly modulated during endocrine differentiation.
source: Furthermore, additional data indicate that ECAD levels are tightly modulated during endocrine differentiation (Gouzi et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study on ECAD regulation during endocrine differentiation

claim: GP2 expression in CD45-CD31- was restricted to the EPCAM+ fraction at 9.4WD.
source: GP2 expression in CD45-CD31- was restricted to the EPCAM+ fraction (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data showing GP2 expression only in EPCAM+ cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1)

claim: GP2 and ECAD expression segregated the CD45-CD31-EPCAM+ fraction into four distinct populations: GP2hiECAD+, GP2+ECAD+, GP2-ECAD+, and GP2-ECADlow at 9.4WD.
source: GP2 and ECAD expression segregated the CD45-CD31-EPCAM+ fraction into four distinct populations: GP2hiECAD+ (named GP2hi), GP2+ECAD+ (named GP2+), GP2-ECAD+ (named GP2-), and the GP2-ECADlow (named Elow) (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry plots showing four distinct populations based on GP2 and ECAD expression (Figure 2A)

claim: The cell frequencies of the four populations (GP2hi, GP2+, GP2-, Elow) were well conserved from one pancreas to the other at 9.4WD, demonstrating inter-individual homogeneity.
source: Remarkably, the cell frequencies of the four populations were well conserved from one pancreas to the other, demonstrating inter-individual homogeneity (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data showing consistent population frequencies across multiple samples (Figure 2B)

claim: At 7WD the epithelial fraction was essentially GP2+ (96 ± 1%).
source: At 7WD the epithelial fraction was essentially GP2+ (96 ± 1%).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry quantification at 7WD (Figure 2C,D)

claim: From 7WD to 8.4WD, the GP2- population evolves from 2 ± 1% to 34 ± 6% (p<0.05).
source: From 7WD to 8.4WD, the GP2- population evolves from 2 ± 1% to 34 ± 6% (p<0.05) (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry quantification showing temporal increase in GP2- population (Figure 2C,D)

claim: From 8.6WD, cells with a lower ECAD level (Elow population) were detected.
source: Interestingly, from 8.6WD, we detected cells with a lower ECAD level (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry showing emergence of ECADlow population at 8.6WD (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B)

claim: The Elow population increased in frequency from 10 ± 2% at 9.4WD to 18 ± 3% at 12WD (p<0.05).
source: This Elow population further increased in frequency from 10 ± 2% at 9.4WD to 18 ± 3% at 12WD (p<0.05) (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry quantification showing temporal increase in Elow population (Figure 2C,D)

claim: At 9.4WD, a GP2hi population was detected, increasing in frequency during development (3 ± 1% at 9.4WD to 20 ± 5% at 12WD; p<0.05).
source: At 9.4WD, we also detected a GP2hi population, increasing in frequency during development (3 ± 1% at 9.4WD to 20 ± 5% at 12WD; p<0.05) (Figure 2C,D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry quantification showing temporal increase in GP2hi population (Figure 2C,D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2C)

claim: The GP2+ population would differentiate either into a GP2hi population or into a GP2- population that would later decrease its ECAD level to give rise to the Elow population.
source: Altogether, the temporal and continuum GP2 and ECAD expression suggest a progeny relationship between specific cell populations, the GP2+ population would differentiate either into a GP2hi population or into a GP2- population that would later decrease its ECAD level to give rise to the Elow population (Figure 2E).
evidence: Based on inference from temporal flow cytometry data showing sequential appearance and changes in population frequencies (Figure 2C,D,E)

claim: Principal component analysis on sorted populations at 9WD revealed three clusters, with PC1 separating the epithelial populations from the mesenchymal fraction, and PC2 segregating the Elow population from the GP2hi, GP2+ and GP2- populations.
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) on the sorted populations at 9WD revealed three clusters. PC1 separated the epithelial populations (GP2hi, GP2+, GP2- and Elow) from the mesenchymal fraction (M), while PC2 segregated the Elow population from the GP2hi, GP2+ and GP2- populations (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by PCA analysis of transcriptomic data (Figure 3A)

claim: Gene Set Enrichment Analysis using Gene Ontology database indicated that digestion was the most represented biological process in the GP2hi and GP2+ populations.
source: Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) using Gene Ontology database indicated that digestion was the most represented biological process in the GP2hi and GP2+ populations while endocrine functions (insulin and peptide secretion, hormone secretion) were enriched in the Elow population (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis of transcriptomic data (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2)

claim: Endocrine functions (insulin and peptide secretion, hormone secretion) were enriched in the Elow population.
source: Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) using Gene Ontology database indicated that digestion was the most represented biological process in the GP2hi and GP2+ populations while endocrine functions (insulin and peptide secretion, hormone secretion) were enriched in the Elow population (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis of transcriptomic data (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2)

claim: The pancreatic functions appeared less enriched in the GP2- population.
source: Conversely the pancreatic functions appeared less enriched in the GP2- population.
evidence: Based on GSEA analysis showing lower enrichment of pancreatic functions in GP2- population compared to other populations (Figure 3B)

claim: The GP2hi population displayed 27 enriched genes (p<0.05), 85% being preferentially expressed in the adult acinar cells.
source: The GP2hi population displayed 27 enriched genes (p<0.05), 85% being preferentially expressed in the adult acinar cells (Figure 3C, and Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Supported by comparison of fetal enriched genes with adult single cell RNAseq data from Segerstolpe et al. (2016) (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 3A)

claim: The Elow population contained 91 (at 9WD) and 34 (at 11WD) differentially expressed genes (p<0.05) that were also enriched (98% and 100% respectively) in the adult endocrine cells.
source: In contrast, the Elow population contained 91 (at 9WD) and 34 (at 11WD) differentially expressed genes (p<0.05) that were also enriched (98% and 100% respectively) in the adult endocrine cells (alpha, beta, delta, epsilon or gamma cells) (Figure 3C, and Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Supported by comparison of fetal enriched genes with adult single cell RNAseq data from Segerstolpe et al. (2016) (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 3B)

claim: Acinar markers such as CEL, CELA3A and CTRC were enriched in the GP2+ population at 9WD and in the GP2hi population at 11WD.
source: By RT-qPCR analyses we confirmed that acinar markers such as CEL, CELA3A and CTRC were enriched in the GP2+ population at 9WD and in the GP2hi population at 11WD (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data showing acinar marker expression in GP2+ and GP2hi populations (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, Figure 4A)

claim: Ductal markers (CFTR, KRT19 and SPP1) were enriched in the GP2+ and GP2- populations, especially CFTR at 9WD and 11-13WD.
source: Ductal markers (CFTR, KRT19 and SPP1) were enriched in the GP2+ and GP2- populations, especially CFTR at 9WD and 11-13WD (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by transcriptomic analysis and RT-qPCR showing ductal marker expression in GP2+ and GP2- populations (Figure 4—figure supplement 1)

claim: The Elow populations (9 and 11WD) were enriched with endocrine transcription factors such as ARX, PAX4, PAX6, NEUROD1, MAFA, MAFB, ISL1 and NKX2.2 and hormones like CHGA, GCG, GHRL and INS.
source: The Elow populations (9 and 11WD) were enriched with endocrine transcription factors such as ARX, PAX4, PAX6, NEUROD1, MAFA, MAFB, ISL1 and NKX2.2 and hormones like CHGA, GCG, GHRL and INS (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B, Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by transcriptomic analysis and RT-qPCR showing endocrine marker expression in Elow population (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B, Figure 4B)

claim: NEUROG3 was first detected at 8.4WD in the GP2- population prior to the detection of the Elow population.
source: NEUROG3 was first detected at 8.4WD in the GP2- population (Figure 4C) prior to the detection of the Elow population (Figure 2C)
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR showing NEUROG3 expression in GP2- population at 8.4WD (Figure 4C) and flow cytometry showing Elow population first detected at 8.6WD (Figure 2C)

claim: NEUROG3 was found enriched in the Elow population from 9 to 13WD.
source: and next (9 to 13WD), found enriched in the Elow population (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR showing NEUROG3 enrichment in Elow population at 9-13WD (Figure 4C)

claim: The first human pancreatic endocrine progenitors differentiate in the GP2- population and mature while decreasing ECAD levels in the Elow population.
source: Thus, our data suggest that the first human pancreatic endocrine progenitors differentiate in the GP2- population and mature while decreasing ECAD levels in the Elow population.

claim: The GP2- population displayed both duct and endocrine progenitor cells markers suggesting it contains more than one cell type.
source: The GP2- population displayed both duct and endocrine progenitor cells markers suggesting it contains more than one cell type.

claim: At 9.4WD, the GP2- and Elow populations were further divided into three subsets: CD142+SUSD2-, CD142-SUSD2- and CD142-SUSD2+.
source: FACS analyses showed that at 9.4WD, the GP2hi and GP2+ populations were uniformly CD142+SUSD2-, while the GP2- and Elow populations were further divided into three subsets: CD142+SUSD2-, CD142-SUSD2- and CD142-SUSD2+ (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry showing CD142 and SUSD2 expression patterns (Figure 5B)

claim: The CD142-SUSD2+ subset was scarce in the GP2- population (6%), but represented 40% of the Elow population at 9.4WD.
source: Noteworthy, the CD142-SUSD2+ subset was scarce in the GP2- population (6%), but represented 40% of the Elow population at 9.4WD (Figure 5B).

source: At 7WD the majority of the GP2- population was CD142+SUSD2- (95 ± 2%).

source: As development progressed the frequency of the ElowCD142-SUSD2+ subset decreased (from 48 ± 7% at 8.6WD to 10 ± 1% at 12WD; p<0.05), while the frequency of the ElowCD142-SUSD2- subset increased (from 30 ± 4% at 8.6WD to 79 ± 3% at 12WD; p<0.05) (Figure 5B,C,E).

source: Moreover, NEUROG3, NEUROD1 and NKX2-2 were mainly expressed in the ECADlowCD142-SUSD2+ population as observed in the human fetal pancreas at 8.6WD (Figures 6A,C and 7D).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR comparing hPSC-derived cells to fetal pancreas (Figures 6A,C and 7D)

claim: From stage 2-5 in hPSC differentiation, the temporal expression pattern of CD142 and ECAD was reminiscent of the ones occurring in the human fetal pancreas with a sharp decrease of CD142+SUSD2- subsets (from 95 ± 2% at stage 2 to 23 ± 4% at stage 5; p<0.05).
source: Finally, from stage 2–5 the temporal expression pattern of CD142 and ECAD was reminiscent of the ones occurring in the human fetal pancreas with a sharp decrease of CD142+SUSD2- subsets (from 95 ± 2 of CD142+SUSD2- at stage 2 to 23 ± 4 of CD142+SUSD2- subset; p<0.05) (5D and 7E)
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry quantification across differentiation stages in three hPSC lines (Figure 7E)

claim: The temporal expression pattern of SUSD2 in hPSC differentiation was similar to that in the human fetal pancreas.
source: as was also the case for SUSD2 expression (Figures 5E and 7F) in the three hPSC lines.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry quantification comparing hPSC differentiation to fetal pancreas development (Figures 5E and 7F)

claim: Pancreatic endocrine cells derived from human pluripotent stem cells appear to go through the same intermediate developmental stages as observed during in vivo development.
source: To conclude we demonstrate that pancreatic endocrine cells derived from human pluripotent stem cells appear to go through the same intermediate developmental stages as observed during in vivo development.
evidence: Based on comparison of marker expression patterns between hPSC-derived cells and fetal pancreas (Figure 7)

claim: The global shape and the way islet cells cluster are different between rodent and human pancreas.
source: For example, the global shape and the way islet cells cluster are different between rodent and human pancreas (Brissova et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to published comparative study

claim: The expression pattern of major transcription factors crucial for proper pancreas development such as NEUROG3, NKX2-2 and PDX1 differ between rodent and human.
source: Moreover, the expression pattern of major transcription factors crucial for proper pancreas development such as NEUROG3, NKX2-2 and PDX1 differ between rodent and human (Villasenor et al., 2008; Salisbury et al., 2014; Jennings et al., 2013; Sussel et al., 1998; Ohlsson et al., 1993; Heimberg et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to published comparative studies

claim: NEUROG3 is expressed in two waves during rodent fetal pancreatic development while only a single-phase is observed in human.
source: As an example, NEUROG3 is expressed in two waves during rodent fetal pancreatic development (Villasenor et al., 2008) while only a single-phase is observed in human (Jennings et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies on NEUROG3 expression patterns

claim: Cells generated in vitro from hPSC do not seem fully differentiated and in some cases, display a fetal phenotype rather than an adult one.
source: However, the cells generated in vitro from hPSC do not seem fully differentiated and in some cases, display a fetal phenotype rather than an adult one. This is the case for hepatocytes (Baxter et al., 2015), cardiomyocytes (Karakikes et al., 2015), neurons (Playne and Connor, 2017) and pancreatic beta cells (Hrvatin et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies on hPSC-derived cell types

claim: The developmental period from 7 to 13WD in human corresponds to E12.5-E17 in the mouse when pancreatic progenitors first proliferate and next develop into differentiated cells.
source: This developmental period corresponds to E12.5-E17 in the mouse when pancreatic progenitors first proliferate and next develop into differentiated cells (Gittes, 2009; Jennings et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies on pancreatic development timing

claim: At 6-7WD, the human pancreatic epithelium is mainly composed of PDX1+NKX6-1+ pancreatic progenitors while endocrine cells are extremely rare.
source: At 6-7WD, the human pancreatic epithelium is mainly composed of PDX1+NKX6-1+ pancreatic progenitors (Cebola et al., 2015; Riedel et al., 2012) while endocrine cells are extremely rare (Polak et al., 2000; Castaing et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies on early human pancreatic development

claim: During the weeks following 7WD, proliferating epithelial pancreatic progenitors differentiate into endocrine, acinar and duct cells.
source: During the following weeks, proliferating epithelial pancreatic progenitors differentiate into endocrine, acinar and duct cells (Jennings et al., 2013; Capito et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies on human pancreatic differentiation

claim: EPCAM is expressed during human fetal life (18-20WD) in the ductal pancreatic epithelium and in developing islet-like cells but also in the adult human pancreas in duct and islet cells.
source: Previous data indicated that EPCAM is expressed during human fetal life (18-20WD) in the ductal pancreatic epithelium and in developing islet-like cells but also in the adult human pancreas in duct and islet cells (Cirulli et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study on EPCAM expression

claim: EPCAM marks the fetal pancreatic epithelium at earlier developmental stages, between 7 and 12WD.
source: Based on this previous report we demonstrated that EPCAM also marks the fetal pancreatic epithelium at earlier developmental stages, between 7 and 12WD.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry and flow cytometry data showing EPCAM expression in pancreatic epithelium at 7-12WD (Figure 1)

claim: The EPCAM+ compartment contains PDX1+NKX6-1+ double-positive cells, a hallmark of pancreatic progenitors.
source: Moreover, we demonstrated that the EPCAM+ compartment contains PDX1+NKX6-1+ double-positive cells, a hallmark of pancreatic progenitors (Jennings et al., 2013; Cebola et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry and RT-qPCR data showing PDX1 and NKX6-1 co-expression in EPCAM+ cells (Figure 1C-F) and citation to published studies on pancreatic progenitor markers

claim: 45% of the EPCAM+ compartment expresses lower levels of PDX1 and NKX6-1.
source: Our data also indicate that 45% of the EPCAM+ compartment expresses lower levels of PDX1 and NKX6-1.
evidence: Based on flow cytometry data showing PDX1 and NKX6-1 expression levels in EPCAM+ cells (Figure 1C-E)

claim: EPCAM+PDX1lowNKX6-1low cells may be upstream progenitors of EPCAM+PDX1+NKX6-1+ cells.
source: It would be interesting to determine if these cells are upstream progenitors of EPCAM+PDX1+NKX6-1+ cells as recently suggested (Ameri et al., 2017).
evidence: Based on speculation supported by citation to published study

claim: GP2 is a glycoprotein that is highly enriched in the acinar cells of the adult pancreas.
source: GP2 is a glycoprotein that is highly enriched in the acinar cells of the adult pancreas (Hoops and Rindler, 1991; Yu et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies on GP2 expression

claim: In the early human fetal pancreas, GP2 is a cell surface marker of a multipotent cell population.
source: Collectively, these data indicate that in the early human fetal pancreas, GP2 is indeed a cell surface marker of a multipotent cell population.
evidence: Based on flow cytometry showing GP2+ cells at 7WD and transcriptomic data showing GP2+ cells can differentiate into multiple lineages (Figure 2, Figure 3)

claim: It is not yet certain if the GP2+ population contains multipotent GP2+ progenitor that can differentiate into the three lineages (endocrine, acinar and ductal) or represent a mixture of GP2+ progenitors already committed to a specific lineage.
source: Although the GP2+ cell population is multipotent, it is not yet certain if the GP2+ population contains multipotent GP2+ progenitor that can differentiate into the three lineages (endocrine, acinar and ductal) or represent a mixture of GP2+ progenitors already committed to a specific lineage.
evidence: Based on speculation about the nature of GP2+ population heterogeneity

claim: During mouse and chick development, Pdx1+Nkx6.1+ progenitors express high levels of ECAD.
source: As an example, during mouse and chick development, Pdx1+Nkx6.1+ progenitors express high levels of ECAD.
evidence: Based on established knowledge from animal model studies

claim: NEUROG3+ endocrine progenitors will develop from pancreatic progenitors while lowering their ECAD level during their delamination from the ductal tree to develop into pancreatic endocrine cells in mouse and chick.
source: NEUROG3+ endocrine progenitors will develop from such pancreatic progenitors while lowering their ECAD level during their delamination from the ductal tree to develop into pancreatic endocrine cells (Gouzi et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study on ECAD regulation during endocrine differentiation

claim: At 7WD, GP2+ pancreatic progenitors express ECAD at high levels in human fetal pancreas.
source: Our results indicate that at 7WD, GP2+ pancreatic progenitors express ECAD at high levels.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data showing ECAD expression in GP2+ cells at 7WD (Figure 2C)

claim: At 8.6WD, ECADlow cells appear in human fetal pancreas, their frequency increasing while development progresses.
source: At 8.6WD, ECADlow cells appear, their frequency increasing while development progresses.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data showing emergence and increase of Elow population (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B)

claim: NEUROG3-expressing cells first appear at 8.4WD in the ECAD+ population and are found later on in the ECADlow population in human fetal pancreas.
source: Interestingly, NEUROG3-expressing cells first appear at 8.4WD in the ECAD+ population and are found later on in the ECADlow population.
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data showing NEUROG3 expression first in GP2- (ECAD+) population at 8.4WD and then in Elow population (Figure 4C)

claim: During mouse development, ECAD function is necessary for proper aggregation of endocrine cells after delamination.
source: This perfectly fits with mouse data that indicate that during development ECAD function is necessary for proper aggregation of endocrine cells after delamination (Dahl et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study on ECAD function in mouse

claim: ECAD levels are tightly regulated during specific steps of human pancreatic development.
source: Taken together, our data demonstrate that ECAD levels are tightly regulated during specific steps of human pancreatic development.
evidence: Based on flow cytometry data showing temporal changes in ECAD expression during development (Figure 2)

claim: CD142 has been proposed as a marker of pancreatic endodermal cells that also labels additional cell types.
source: CD142 has been proposed as a marker of pancreatic endodermal cells that also labels additional cell types (Kelly et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study on CD142 as a pancreatic marker

claim: SUSD2 was previously used as a marker to enrich NEUROG3+ from hPSC derived pancreatic cells and the human fetal pancreas.
source: SUSD2 was previously used as a marker to enrich NEUROG3+ from hPSC derived pancreatic cells and the human fetal pancreas (Liu et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study on SUSD2 as a marker for NEUROG3+ cells

claim: GP2+CD142+ pancreatic progenitors can either give rise to GP2hiCD142+ acinar cells or enter the endocrine pathway and express NEUROG3 by turning off GP2 and CD142.
source: Our data indicate that GP2+CD142+ pancreatic progenitors can either give rise to GP2hiCD142+ acinar cells or enter the endocrine pathway and express NEUROG3 by turning off GP2 and CD142.
evidence: Based on inference from temporal marker expression data (Figure 2, Figure 4C, Figure 5)

claim: Differences in gene expression and functionality were observed between fetal, neonatal and adult beta cells.
source: Recently, differences in gene expression and functionality were observed between fetal, neonatal and adult beta cells (Hrvatin et al., 2014; Jermendy et al., 2011; Blum et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies on beta cell heterogeneity across developmental stages

claim: Heterogeneity between adult beta cells was recently described.
source: Moreover, heterogeneity between adult beta cells was also recently described (Dorrell et al., 2016; Bader et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies on adult beta cell heterogeneity

claim: A combination of CD49f and CD133 antibodies can be used to enrich fraction in mouse pancreatic progenitors expressing NEUROG3-expressing cells with some data on human fetal pancreas.
source: It was found that a combination of CD49f and CD133 antibodies can be used to enrich fraction in mouse pancreatic progenitors expressing NEUROG3-expressing cells with some data on human fetal pancreas.
evidence: Based on general knowledge of published studies on pancreatic cell surface markers

claim: The enrichment in NEUROG3 on human fetal pancreas was limited using the combination of CD49f and CD133 markers.
source: However, the enrichment in NEUROG3 on human fetal pancreas was limited using this combination of markers (Sugiyama et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study on CD49f and CD133 markers

claim: SUSD2 does not mark all, but only a subset of NEUROG3+ that co-expressed NEUROD1 and NKX2-2.
source: However our single cell qPCR indicate that SUSD2 does not mark all, but only a subset of NEUROG3+ that co-expressed NEUROD1 and NKX2-2.
evidence: Supported by single cell RT-qPCR data showing NEUROG3+ cells in both SUSD2+ and SUSD2- subsets (Figure 6D,E)

claim: By using a combination of antibodies against cell surface markers, cell populations highly enriched in specific functions can be sorted from the human fetal pancreas at different stages of development.
source: Thus, by using a combination of antibodies against cell surface markers, we demonstrate that cell populations highly enriched in specific functions can be sorted from the human fetal pancreas at different stages of development, allowing the reconstruction of the differentiation program.
evidence: Based on flow cytometry, transcriptomic, and RT-qPCR data showing functional enrichment in sorted populations (Figures 1-6)

claim: The development model described for human fetal pancreas also applies to the in vitro differentiation of hPSCs into pancreatic endocrine cells.
source: We further refined our work for the endocrine pathway by describing for the first time, discrete stages of human pancreatic endocrine cell differentiation and showed that our development model also applies to the in vitro differentiation of hPSCs into pancreatic endocrine cells.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry and RT-qPCR data comparing hPSC-derived cells to fetal pancreas (Figure 7)

claim: This type of side-by-side comparison demonstrating that in vitro hPSC differentiation mimics in vivo events has rarely been done.
source: To the best of our knowledge, this type of side-by-side comparison that demonstrates that in vitro hPSC differentiation mimics in vivo events has rarely been done.
evidence: Based on authors' knowledge of the field

claim: Human fetal pancreases were isolated from surgical abortion done by suction aspiration between 7 to 13 weeks of development in compliance with the French bioethics legislation and the guidelines of the institution.
source: Human fetal pancreases were isolated from surgical abortion done by suction aspiration between 7 to 13 weeks of development (Castaing et al., 2001; Capito et al., 2013; Scharfmann et al., 2014) in compliance with the French bioethics legislation and the guidelines of our institution.
evidence: Statement of experimental procedures and ethical compliance

claim: Approval was obtained from Agence de Biomedecine, the French competent authority along with maternal written consent for use of human fetal pancreases.
source: Approval was obtained from Agence de Biomedecine, the French competent authority along with maternal written consent.
evidence: Statement of ethical approval and consent

claim: Ages of human fetal pancreases were determined on the basis of time since the last menstrual period and hand and foot morphology.
source: Ages were determined on the basis of time since the last menstrual period and hand and foot morphology.
evidence: Statement of methodology for determining fetal age
